The Tunnel Disaster.
Special Dispatch to The Bee.

New York, August 2, 4 p. m.—Work on the cofferdam by which the twenty bodies buried in the Hudson river tunnel at Jersey City, were to be recovered, went on slowly yesterday. One of the men in charge of that portion of the work, stated that the cofferdam has proved impractically and that they could go no further with it than they had, for the reason that they could no longer control the water. It is now the intention to sink a caisson on the site of the present cofferdam using compressed air.

Satisfied Coal Miners.
Special Dispatch to The Bee.

MASSILLON, O., August 2—4 p. m.—The coal miners of Tuscarorias valley have wheeled into line and rejected the resolutions of the inter-state conventions, held at Pittsburg in March and at Columbus last month. The rejected resolutions demanded the abolition of screens, eight hours for a day's work and two pay days a month. John McBride, state president, says the prospects are good for steady work here for a year or two, and that the present arrangement gives general satisfaction among the men.

NEW YORK, August 3.--A Nashville special states that a party of negroes gathered in front of the house of a man named Harry Crenshaw at Woodland Mills, Obion county, Sunday night and commenced cursing and using obscene language. Crenshaw went out to demonstrate against their disorderly conduct, and ordered them to cease their noise. This enraged the negroes to such an extent that they commenced blackguarding him, when he shot into the crowd. Alexander Ellison, one of the negroes, returned the fire, emptying the contents of a double barreled shotgun into Crenshaw's breast and stomach. Crenshaw fell to the ground and was taken into the house to die. STABBING AFFRAY.

LAFAYETTE, Ind., Aug. 2. James Farrell last night became involved in a quarrel with Stephen Gaston, during which the latter drew a knife and inflicted eight or nine ugly-looking gashes on Farrell's body. One across the abdomen is considered very dangerous, and the chances are that he will die, should inflammation set in. Gaston was the engineer at the distillery, and Farrell was a discharged fireman. Gaston claims that he was at the distillery, when Farrell came in and assaulted him, and he cut him with the knife, he being engaged in whittling at the time. Gaston surrendered himself, and was let go, but this morning Farrell's condition was regarded as dangerous, and he was locked up. Since his arrest Gaston declines to make any statement, save that it was self-defense.

HARRY CRENSHAW SHOT BY A COLORED MAN.—On Sunday night last, Mr. Harry Crenshaw, a citizen of Woodland Mills, Tenn., was shot (and seriously wounded) by a negro known as Alex Elison. Crenshaw was a quick, impulsive, but in every respect an exemplary citizen, and the circumstances of his killing produced the highest excitement and indignation. The negro, in company with quite a squad, were indulging in a general spree, disturbing the peace, and using much loud, boisterous and profane language, directly in front of Crenshaw's family residence, when Crenshaw protested to the negroes, and told them they must stop it. The negro Alec replied in a drunken, insulting manner, defying Crenshaw to come out of his own yard and try to stop it. Crenshaw got his gun, accompanied by two young white men, started across the fence to quiet the disturbance, when the negro Alec, who was provided with a shot gun, fired upon him emptying 25 shot into Crenshaw's legs and abdomen. Deaf and Dumb Negro Killed.
Bluford Workman, colored, deaf mute, was found dead in a cotton patch near the roadside opposite Mr. Barnett Floyd's Friday morning, having been killed the night previous. He was shot with a pistol of about 40 calibre; the ball entered below the right shoulder, passed through the heart and stopped just under the skin of the left breast, where it was taken out by Dr. Thompson. Coroner Longshore held an inquest over the body Friday, and on account of the absence of some witnesses he adjourned it over to Saturday and again to Monday. We have not learned the verdict of the jury. The deceased was twenty-three years old, and formerly belonged to Mr. Madison Workman. At the time of his death he was in the employ of Mr. Charley Floyd. He was a peaceable and harmless negro. From what we have learned the killing seems to have been a horrible outrage, without the slightest provocation. We do not propose, in advance of the verdict of the Coroner's jury, to give any of the rumors that are floating around, but only to say that there should be a strict, impartial and thorough investigation of this matter; that the officers of the law must do their duty fearlessly and without favor, and that the guilty party should be brought to justice.

We understand that the verdict of the Coroner's Jury yesterday (Monday) afternoon was, that the deceased was killed by C. D. Burton in self-defense.

GEN, BUTLER ON GEN, CASH,
Comments of the Senator Upon the Letter to the National Republican.
Correspondence of the News and Courier.
COUNTRY AUGUST 18 HANDBOOK

Columbia, August 12.—Having occasion to visit Edgefield your Reporter called upon Senator Butler with a copy of Col. Cash's letter as it appeared in the National Republican, and inquired if he had anything further to say about it.

The Senator had not seen the note to the Postmaster at Washington, and when he had read it, smiled and remarked that he had never objected to the publication of the letter; on the contrary, was quite willing that it should be published. Col. Cash was entitled to have a say, and now that he had delivered himself he hoped he would be in a better frame of mind. "But," said the Senator, "just how it could injure the Democratic party I cannot see, and therefore cannot understand why any paper should have refused to publish the letter on that account. If Col. Cash finds the Radical party more congenial—appearing from his note to have fallen out with the Democratic party—it is entirely proper for him to seek comfort in its ranks. Such a consummation appears to be in accordance with the 'eternal fitness of things.'"

REPORTER: Have you anything to say, General, in reply to the charges which Col. Cash brings against you?

GEN. BUTLER: No, except to say that they are purely imaginary. Not a word of truth in any of them. Of course, I do not say whether his charge, that I am a coward, is true or not. It is never safe to pass judgment on any man's courage. I have seen some people terribly disappointed in that regard, and Col. Cash may find it so in this case, but we cannot always tell.

REP.: Have you ever had any moneyed transactions with him? What does he mean by "the privilege of inserting your hands in his pockets," &c., &c.

GEN. B.: Why, it means that the man is crazy or something worse. I never had a moneyed transaction, or endeavored to have one with him in my life, nor any other business transaction. So he has drawn entirely on his imagination for this statement. Nor did I ever "piteously apply" to him about the "lottery," as he calls it. My own and Gen. Gary's connection with that business has been explained again and again, and was about the same as that of Gens. Beauregard and Early with the Louisiana lottery. The difference is, that theirs has been a success, ours was a stupendous failure. Our attempting such an enterprise; under the circumstances, was a piece of ineffable stupidity, but I had no occasion to apply piteously to Col. Cash or anybody else about it, and, therefore, his statement in regard to it is without foundation in fact. Like every man who makes such a mistake, I felt disgusted with myself about it, but I had no in the habit of complaining of sympathy being withheld as Col. Cash does in my case.

REP.: He says that you had "recently been branded in public as a liar, and only sought redress by returning the offensive epithet." Did such an occurrence ever take place?

GEN. B.: Never. There is not a word of truth in it. And I have only this to say as to that. If Col. Cash will produce one respectable or reputable man who will say that such a thing happened, if I do not prove that he lies I will make to him the most object apology for any grievance, real or imaginary, that was ever made to man. And if he does not do so where will he be? Oh, no. I have no objection to the publication of the letter. Very hard things have been said about me before and I have survived them and I trust I will survive this. There are some things that I might say about the publication of my letter, but I shall not do so now; nor shall I indulge in recriminations with Col. Cash, or throw mud at him, but leave him to his own conscience, which I hope will cause him to feel ashamed of his letter. He was not in the "letters of the law" when my letter was written, to my knowledge, and they do not appear to chafe much now. I have nothing to retract of my letter, but cannot see why Col. Cash should feel specially aggrieved, as no more mention is made of him than others connected with the duel, unless the "cap fits him" better than others, for which I am not to blame. I only expressed my opinion about a public transaction in which a number of persons were engaged. Why, have I not the right to do that?

Editor Chronicle:
The Natchitoches Register publishes a letter from a correspondent relative to the killing of Harry Wheeler, the negro who killed Mr. Thos. Phillips, which states that his wife was also found dead, and supposes that she was thrown from a horse and killed. This version of the affair leaves the matter in doubt as to the cause of her death, and of course the impression naturally occurs that she was killed by the citizens in pursuit of Wheeler. On the contrary from this, Wheeler's wife is now living on Little river, in Natchitoches parish. The Register's correspondent was misinformed of the affair, or purposely added the statement of the woman being killed merely for political effect, thereby imposing upon the Register, as we know that paper would not put forth a slander against this people. We specially desire it to be remembered that the citizens of this parish have not so far forgot themselves as to kill a woman under any ciscumstances. I do not suppose there was a citizen in pursuit of Wheeler who would not have killed him upon sight, or the smallest excuse in the way of resistance, so cowardly and unprovoked was the murder. Tom Phillips was raised here and was well known. He was a brave man, and when the war opened he volunteered, leaving here in Capt. McCain's company of the 12th Louisiana Volunteer Infantry. He served through the entire war, and was never known to shirk his duty as a soldier. He was at the battles of Franklin, Peach Tree Creek, Nashville, Atlanta and many others. Major McCain and others who served with him state that it was a notorious fact that he seldom if ever missed a roll call, or any part of his duty. As a soldier he was brave to a fault, as a citizen he was an exemplary one. Why, then, should we not be justly incensed at these statements regarding his death and that of his murderer? To those who blotted out Harry Wheeler's existence, we can say, "Gentlemen, you did your duty, and the people will stand by you." Trusting all misrepresentations will be duly corrected and the affair set at rest, I remain yours respectfully. M. A. D.

A SLANDER REFUTED.
Full Particulars of the Killing of the Negro Harry Wheeler.
MONTGOMERY, August 10, 1880.
Editor Chronicle:
We have seen your issue of August 7th, and noted your article replying to We The People, which is a true and correct statement. The facts are simply, that a negro named Harry Wheeler, a cropper on the plantation of Thomas Phillips, about five miles from this place, shot and killed said Thomas Phillips on July 6, 1880. An inquest was held by S. C. Curry, justice of the peace for ward 7; the jury declared that Mr. Phillips came to his death from a gun shot wound, inflicted by a shot gun in the hands of Harry Wheeler, colored. Upon this verdict a warrant was issued and placed in the hands of an officer for execution. The officer failing to find the negro, a posse was called out and the country searched, but the criminal escaped from this vicinity and wandered through the woods toward the Mississippi river, where he has kindred. He was seen and pursued, and just one week after the murder was perpetrated, he was overtaken and surrounded at Lacroix's Ferry, on Little river, in the extreme eastern end of Grant parish. The wish was general that he should be captured and brought back, but when the posse came in sight, the negro drew his knife, and with it in one hand and a double-barreled shot gun in the other, broke to run. The posse halted him repeatedly, so often and for so long a time that he got so far off that when shots were fired at him he was untouched. But he was not to escape. Other parties had taken position in the surrounding and as he ran to escape he came in their range, when they opened fire on him, shooting him through body and brain. He fell, dying instantly. An inquest was held by the justice of ward 2, after which the body was coffined and buried in a graveyard near the ferry.

The wife of the negro Wheeler is now living with her children on the plantation of Col. Thompson, in the parish of Natchitoches, not more than seven miles from where Mr. Phillips was murdered. It will be useless for the Radical party, or Mad. Wells, or We The People, or any agent of the above in this parish, to make any political or bloody shirt outrage from the facts in this case. Instead, the proceedings, from first to last, have been by authority, legal and deliberate, no effort being made by the citizens except in furtherance of justice and order according to law.
H. V. McCain & Bro., R. B. Williams,
A. V. Ragan, C. C. Dunn,
W. O. Harrison, J. S. Payne,
W. M. Watson, Jules Lameraux.

HALIFAX CITY, Va., Aug. 7.—For three days past the colored people in this vicinity have been holding a series of religious meetings in the woods, which they call "bush meetings." AN EXTRAORDINARY CONFESSION.

[Special Telegram to the Globe.]

DETROIT, Mich., Aug. 8.—Mrs. Smith, who died in the Detroit prison yesterday, made a most extraordinary ante mortem confession Friday to the matron of that institution. On the night of the 13th of September, 1876, her husband was murdered as he lay in bed beside her. The body was then taken to the barn, which was set on fire. Mrs. Smith, her sister, her sister's husband and a young farm hand named Alexander turned State's evidence, the former swearing that her husband was killed by her brother-in-law and her sister, whom she incited to the deed. Both were found guilty and sentenced to State prison for life. Mrs. Smith was given fifteen years imprisonment and young Alexander ten. In her confession to the hospital matron Mrs. Smith said she swore falsely, that neither of the parties convicted had anything to do with the crime, nor did she know who committed it. She says that a certain party, whose name has not been revealed by the authorities, persuaded her to make the false confession assuring her that she would receive a light sentence. In her anxiety to rejoin her children she agreed to do as was suggested. While giving her testimony she was under the direction of this party, who was in the court room at the trial. At certain preconcerted signs made by him she answered "yes" or "no" to the questions of the prosecuting attorney. The confession creates considerable of a sensation in Detroit and the matter will doubtless lead to a searching investigation.

POISONED WATERMELONS.

[Special Telegram to the Globe.]

HALIFAX CITY, Va., Aug. 8.—For three days past the colored people in the vicinity have been holding a series of religious meetings, which they call "bush meetings." These gatherings were held near Mr. Brash's watermelon patch, and he noticed that suddenly his melons were disappearing, and he connected their disappearance with the presence of the association. He said nothing, but day before yesterday put up several large placards in his patch with a notice. "Look out! These watermelons are poisoned." INDIANA.

Special Correspondence of The Chicago Tribune.

LAFAYETTE, Ind., Aug. 20.—The corn-crop of Tippecanoe County may be said to have gone up the spout. The early rains drowned out nearly everything. Then the weeds got such a start as to discourage the farmers. The excessive rains were followed by an exceedingly long spell of dry weather; and now the corn is well nigh burned up, or so badly stunted as to be scarcely fit for fodder. In Lauranile Township, for instance, there has not been rain sufficient to lay the dust since the 2d of June. Fields which last year yielded forty and fifty bushels to the acre will not yield one-fifth that amount this year. Many farmers will not raise sufficient corn for their own use, and, unless they have a surplus from the year before, will have to go into the market. The potatoes have all dried out, and many of the fields will hardly pay for the digging.

MINNESOTA AND DAKOTA.

Special Dispatch to The Chicago Tribune.
LA Crosse, Wis., Aug. 30.—The prospects for a large crop of wheat in the western portion of Southern Minnesota and Dakota have been somewhat lessened by the constant rains of the past week. In many places the wheat lays on the ground cut, and the rain has caused considerable damage. In the majority of places it is still in the shock, not having been stacked. The lack of help and carolessness is attributed to this neglect. The harvest is very backward compared with the last few years. The yield in places where wheat has been thrashed is considerably below the estimate of the yield. In fact, first reports from that section of a heavy yield are exaggerated. Corn is looking fine, with prospects for a large yield.

ALONG THE NORTHERN PACIFIC. Chicago, Aug. 30.—Careful examination of the condition of the wheat crop in the great wheat belt on the line of the Northern Pacific Railroad has been made for the Associated Press, and it can be stated that reports of its being in danger in consequence of wet weather are unwarranted. The late spring delayed seeding and harvest fully two weeks, and the last week of cloudy weather along the line has interfered with thrashing, but the crop is safe, and with favorable weather will commence moving largely this week, fully three weeks later, however, than last year. The Dalrymple farm alone will require thirty-five cars a day to take care of the grain as thrashed.
